RagShortTexts: Lingonberries supply seasonal food, with storage and exchange limited by weather and vessels.
Cold-injured people need shelter, dry clothes and care rather than a guaranteed berry cure.

Variants.Content:
Woodland lingonberries and other berries provide food to eat or store, depending on ripeness, weather and place. Pressure releases juice, while leaks and spoiled fruit reduce what reaches home. Keeping, gifting or trading the harvest depends on grain and access to market; sour flavour does not replace bread or porridge.

Cold-weather gatherers face wet feet, wind and delayed returns. Numb hands and feet or damaged skin impair future work. Families offer available food to sufferers, who still need shelter, dry clothing, nourishment and continuing care. Fruit pulp on an injury does not establish recovery, and pain, inability to walk or worsening illness requires further help.
Forest dues should not force dangerous returns. Cold injuries reduce labour, and food, shelter and relief from duties matter beyond a jar of fruit.
Scouts need dry foot coverings and should not fall behind for berries. Unsteady companions or failing fingers call for shelter and help.
Gathering families share work according to strength. Bringing a cold-injured person home needs carts, clothes and help with missed chores.
